title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Facing the reality of death enables people to appreciate the importance of living, inspiring them to develop a whole new way to make…
content:
Death as a Teacher of Wise Living and Presence

"Facing the reality of death enables people to appreciate the importance of living, inspiring them to develop a whole new way to make the best use of the valuable time they have left. They learn to value the reflection on death and make it a daily practice, fostering the awareness that each day could be their last. The Buddha strongly emphasized death contemplation to spur people toward genuine spiritual practice. When you know that death is certain but its timing is uncertain, you naturally want to put your house in order. You stop postponing your meditation, stop making excuses, and stop waiting for some perfect future moment that never arrives. In this way, death is a profound teacher. When you truly understand that each moment could be your last, you start paying attention to how you live. You become more careful with your speech, more mindful of your actions, and more aware of the moods of your mind. You start living with purpose instead of just passing time."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "From the point of view of the true citta these things are peripheral. The true citta is the citta free from defilements and…
content:
The Citta as the Central Basis of Existence

"From the point of view of the true citta these things are peripheral. The true citta is the citta free from defilements and avijjā. It is difficult to realise how everything we do, think, or remember or feel requires the activity of the citta. Mostly we are so involved with things in the world that we forget ourselves and we forget the citta and the fundamental basis of our existence. For it is the function of the citta which knows, cognises, and experiences everything, rightly or wrongly as it may be. Therefore, the citta is the centre and everything else is peripheral. Usually people think that they have a citta, but this is the wrong way around. We should perhaps ask whether the citta has the person."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "There may be things that you haven’t really understood which you suddenly see a connection between, making you understand how they fit together…
content:
The Natural Growth of Practice

"There may be things that you haven’t really understood which you suddenly see a connection between, making you understand how they fit together – like a gearbox, they're the right shapes and sizes so they all slide in and out together. Ajaan Mahā Boowa talks about planting a tree. When you plant a tree you can't make it grow faster than it naturally will. All you can do is give it the right conditions, then it grows at its own rate. It’s the same with our development in Dhamma. You can continue to do what's necessary in the practice to develop in the Dhamma, and it will grow, but at its own rate. Some people grow faster and some slower."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Fundamentally, the teaching of Buddhism deals with oneself. We all have a big problem, and Buddhism teaches us how to correct that problem.…
content:
Discontent as the Universal Human Problem

"Fundamentally, the teaching of Buddhism deals with oneself. We all have a big problem, and Buddhism teaches us how to correct that problem. The problem is discontent or suffering. Discontent is always there in our lives; in little thing and big things, always in some way we’re dissatisfied. When we want something, we want it only because we don’t have it. That lack creates a state of disharmony inside which expresses itself as dukkha or discontent. Our habitual reaction is to search for something to overcome that disharmony within ourselves. Because of that, we’re always searching, always looking for things. This constant searching is a major source of frustration, because whatever solution we find is never quite satisfactory. This in fact is the fundamental problem of all people; not just Buddhists, but everybody throughout the world."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "The most important faculty used to overcome the kilesas is mindfulness. There is little doubt about that. Mindfulness is the best tool you…
content:
Using Mindfulness to Interrupt the Cycle of Craving

"The most important faculty used to overcome the kilesas is mindfulness. There is little doubt about that. Mindfulness is the best tool you have. Mindfulness automatically tends to show you where the kilesas are and how they operate. When you are always watchful, keeping an eye on them, the kilesas cannot easily get a grip on you. To overcome the kilesas, you must go directly at taṇhā, craving. The craving is the trouble. By overcoming craving, you overcome attachments. But you cannot deal with the attachments directly. Trying to overcome attachments by will power or by sheer determination does not work. To get rid of the attachments you must first get rid of their cause. The cause of attachments is taṇhā, craving. You see it in the Paticcasamuppada. Taṇhā is the condition for the arising of attachment. When you get rid of the taṇhā, the attachment cannot arise. And if you want to get rid of the taṇhā, you have to watch the feeling, because feeling is the condition for taṇhā. That is a very important point, because exactly at that point you can put a barrier between the feeling and taṇhā."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: What actually happens is invariably quite complex. What’s really happening is more like a whirlpool, a whirlpool of constant change. If we try…
content:
Seeing Through the Whirlpool of Constant Change

What actually happens is invariably quite complex. What’s really happening is more like a whirlpool, a whirlpool of constant change. If we try to resist change and remain static, we will miss the truth every time. If we can just watch it closely, we will see that everything is part of this whirlpool of changing phenomena. So we let it follow its natural tendency. We should try to be aware that there is a vortex of activity occurring in and around us all the time. We experience this, but because our minds are not quick enough to catch up with the constant arising and ceasing of phenomena, we have to reduce the whole lot to something simple enough for our minds to latch on to. Thus we create a symbol. For instance, a motorcar. The word “motorcar” is just a symbol. What is a car actually? It’s an assemblage of 100,000 different parts. Nevertheless, we represent it with that one symbol. Similarly, a “house” is composed of countless bits and pieces. We refer to it as a house because our minds just aren’t capable of handling the complexity of what’s really there. We just can’t hold it all in our minds at the same time, so we have to simplify.

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Standing as a hindrance to that effort is the fact that many people feel they have a right to be angry, and because…
content:
The Illusion of Justified Anger and the Power of Mindful Observation

"Standing as a hindrance to that effort is the fact that many people feel they have a right to be angry, and because of that, they believe that their anger is not really wrong. They justify their anger by blaming others for intentionally doing things to make them angry. It is always someone else's fault. 'Don't blame me,' they say. The problem is, when people act out their angry emotions, they are likely to receive an angry response in return. Even if they feel completely justified in their anger, expressing it usually creates more conflict and pain and does nothing to solve the original problem. On the other hand, calmly observing others' behavior with mindful awareness, instead of immediate judgment or anger, can lead to better relationships and less suffering for everyone involved. Even though we think we have good reasons for communicating our displeasure, all anger directed at others—no matter how justified or how righteous it may appear—originates from unwholesome feelings of aversion and hatred. Whether angry actions are expressed in violent ways or nonviolent ways, the effect is still harmful, and displays of anger will never bring about circumstances leading to forgiveness and reconciliation."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Mettā is the most powerful practice of the lot. Mettā is the strongest thing and because of that a lot of people are…
content:
The Power and Internal State of Mettā

"Mettā is the most powerful practice of the lot. Mettā is the strongest thing and because of that a lot of people are frightened of mettā. They don't know how to behave. If you have mettā for someone what you're doing by having mettā for that person is putting your own citta into a state of mettā. This is the important part. If the citta is not in a state of mettā then you won't help anyone else. By the attitude of having them in mind that can have an influence on that person. By the power of that influence their minds can be put in the same sort of state. Then they can build up good kamma on that. The mettā is an influence on that other person. Some people get the idea they're mettā broadcasting stations. They don't realize that the mettā first of all must be inside."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "You will find that anxiety arises initially as feeling, so you must look at that feeling. But first you must acknowledge, quite honestly,…
content:
Investigating Anxiety and Finding Its Physical Focal Point

"You will find that anxiety arises initially as feeling, so you must look at that feeling. But first you must acknowledge, quite honestly, that you have anxiety, and don't try to resist it in anyway. Once you have acknowledged the anxiety, you can turn to investigate it with an open mind. Examine exactly how the state of anxiety comes up. You feel anxiety, so what is it that tells you that you have anxiety? What is that quality within yourself that you know as anxiety? In what way does it announce itself? When you investigate that thoroughly, you will probably find one spot, or one of feeling, in the body that is its focal point. From then on, when ever anxiety comes up, you can go straight to that point and deal with it directly."

title: A. Paññāvaddho: "Fundamentally [kilesas] mean greed, hatred and delusion, but when approaching them from your own experience, you will see the kilesas are mainly what…
content:
Understanding the Motives of Kilesas

"Fundamentally [kilesas] mean greed, hatred and delusion, but when approaching them from your own experience, you will see the kilesas are mainly what you are and the way you think and the motives that you have. That’s where the kilesas will be found. When you look at them closely you will see that the kilesas are always associated with 'I' or self. I think like that. I feel it in this way. There is always the self perspective coming up. And the kilesas come up with self in order to push self higher. And the more that self is pushed up, the more gratified we feel. Of course, when the self gets pushed up high, it can easily fall down. When it falls down, there is dukkha. When a person pushes self up very high, conceit is the consequence. When the conceit is toppled, that’s real suffering."
